title: Heterogeneously Integrated Efficient and Widely Tunable Lasers at 795 nm for Rubidium-Based Quantum Technologies
authors: Max Kiewiet, Stijn Cuyvers, Tom Reep, Konstantinos Akritidis, Gaudhaman Jeevanandam, Manuel Reza, Roelof Jansen, Pol Van Dorpe, Günther Roelkens, Kasper Van Gasse, Bart Kuyken
abstract: Scaling quantum processors and optical atomic clocks fundamentally requires orders-of-magnitude reductions in the size, weight, power, and cost of optical control systems. Photonic integration of lasers is critical to fulfill these requirements. At the near-infrared wavelengths required for atomic clocks and quantum computing through manipulation of rubidium atoms, laser integration is hindered by difficulty in light coupling and poor heat dissipation. Here, we introduce a wafer-scalable method utilizing micro-transfer printing to integrate GaAs-based amplifiers in etched recesses, directly butt-coupled to silicon nitride waveguides. We demonstrate extended-cavity single-mode lasers using this integration approach. Our compact microgear laser achieves a narrow 3 kHz fundamental linewidth at an on-chip output power of >22 mW -- a record for a single-mode heterogeneously integrated laser in the 780-800 nm band -- with a wall-plug efficiency of 9.4%, showcasing the high-power and efficiency potential of this integration approach. Additionally, we demonstrate a widely tunable laser leveraging Vernier filters to achieve lasing with 9 nm coarse tuning, a quasi-continuous fine-tuning range exceeding 140 GHz, and a mode-hop-free tuning range of 45 GHz. Our scalable integrated laser toolkit shows great promise for replacing macroscopic external-cavity diode lasers in next-generation quantum technologies and optical atomic clocks.
summary: This paper presents a breakthrough in integrating high-performance lasers onto silicon nitride platforms using micro-transfer printing. The resulting compact, tunable, and efficient laser toolkit is specifically designed to replace bulky external lasers for next-generation quantum technologies and optical atomic clocks utilizing Rubidium atoms.
main_problem: Scaling quantum processors and optical atomic clocks requires drastically reducing the size, weight, power, and cost of optical control systems by integrating lasers.
main_result: The authors demonstrated a highly efficient, compact, and tunable integrated laser source capable of operating at the required near-infrared wavelengths for Rubidium quantum technologies.
method: They developed a wafer-scalable method using micro-transfer printing to butt-couple GaAs-based amplifiers into silicon nitride waveguides, forming extended-cavity single-mode lasers.
model_or_system: The platform integrates III-V semiconductor amplifiers (RSOAs) into a silicon nitride (SiN) waveguide structure. The laser functionality is realized using a microgear reflector structure for single-mode operation and Vernier filters for tunability.
key_observables: Narrow fundamental linewidth (3 kHz), on-chip output power (>22 mW), high wall-plug efficiency (9.4%), and wide tuning ranges (e.g., 140 GHz fine-tuning).
important_parameters: Target wavelength of 795 nm (for Rubidium D1 line); the integration technique overcomes thermal dissipation issues associated with traditional wafer bonding.
main_assumptions: The MTP technique is superior to traditional bonding methods due to better heat sinking and coupling efficiency; future work requires optimizing the SiN cavity design and adding heaters for full resonance tuning.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the schematic applications for Rb spectroscopy, the detailed MTP integration process, and the measured performance characteristics of the microgear and tunable lasers.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the need for photonic integration, details the MTP fabrication process for coupling GaAs to SiN, presents characterization results for the narrow-linewidth microgear laser, and then demonstrates the versatility of the platform using a widely tunable Vernier laser.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the hardware bottleneck for quantum information processing and optical metrology by providing a compact, high-performance, and scalable light source tailored for atomic physics experiments.
